a: Before there is a chip there is a hole in the ground. The AI economy begins as quartz, ore, gas and water — a handful of which come from effectively one place on Earth.
Purification is the real magic trick. Ordinary sand becomes silicon with fewer than one foreign atom per billion, and the chemicals that touch a wafer are purer than anything else humans make.
A single crystal is pulled from the melt as one continuous lattice, sliced into 300 mm mirrors, and handed to the fab as the flattest mass-produced object in existence.
Nobody draws 200 billion transistors. They are compiled — from architecture and IP blocks, through synthesis and place-and-route, into a mask description that no human ever reads.

Light is the sculptor. A tin droplet blasted twice by a CO₂ laser makes 13.5 nm photons that bounce off the smoothest mirrors ever built, through a mask, onto resist. This is the industry's deepest moat.
A leading-edge wafer runs 1,000–1,500 process steps over three to four months: deposit an atomic layer, pattern it, etch it away, polish flat, repeat several hundred times.
The transistor itself — now a stack of gate-all-around nanosheets, soon with power delivered from the back of the wafer. Node names stopped being dimensions and became brands a decade ago.
Compute is not the bottleneck; feeding it is. High-bandwidth memory — DRAM dies stacked twelve high over through-silicon vias — is the scarcest strategic component in AI hardware.
When a single die can no longer hold the design, you stitch several together on a silicon interposer. Advanced packaging, not lithography, is the binding constraint on AI accelerator supply.
The accelerator: tens of thousands of tiny matrix engines, a memory hierarchy engineered around them, and a numeric format shrinking from 32 bits toward 4 to buy more arithmetic per joule.
One chip is useless. The interesting object is 72 GPUs behaving as one, and then 100,000 of those behaving as one — which is a networking problem masquerading as a compute problem.
Racks are now the unit of sale. A modern AI rack is 1.5 tonnes of copper busbar, cold plate and midplane assembled by contract manufacturers you have probably never heard of.
Electricity, not silicon, is the binding constraint on the build-out. Interconnection queues run five to seven years, so the industry is quietly building its own private grid.
Two thousand watts through a package the size of a postcard cannot be air-cooled. The industry has reluctantly returned to plumbing after thirty years of fans.
The data centre: land, power, water, fibre and politics, financed through structures that increasingly resemble project finance for a power plant rather than IT procurement.
Turning a warehouse of accelerators into a machine that can run for weeks without losing a training job — scheduling, storage, health checks and checkpoints.
The software that makes silicon fast: compilers, hand-tuned kernels, collective libraries and parallelism strategies. This layer is the most underrated moat in the entire stack.
Models are compressed experience. Where that experience comes from — crawled, licensed, generated or paid for by the hour — is now a contested market and a contested legal question.
Attention, mixtures of experts, and a training recipe: predict the next token at enormous scale, then spend months teaching the result to be useful, honest and safe.
You cannot ship what you cannot measure. Evaluation, red-teaming, interpretability and security are the quality-control layer of an industry whose product is probabilistic.
Training is a capital event; inference is the business. Serving economics — cache, batch, quantise, route — decide whether a product has gross margins.
A model that can call tools, read a repository, browse, remember and hand work to another model stops being a chatbot and becomes a coworker with a very short memory.
Where tokens meet a job to be done. The application layer is growing revenue faster than any software category in history — and burning through model providers' margins to do it.
Physical AI: the same architectures pointed at joints, wheels and grippers, where being wrong has consequences that no retry button can undo.
The last centimetre — chat windows, IDEs, browsers, phones and glasses. Distribution decides which model a billion people actually touch.
The money and the rules. Roughly $700bn of capex in 2026, financed by everything from sovereign funds to asset-backed debt, inside an export-control regime that redraws itself every few months.
The last consumer of value — and everything the chain leaves behind: depreciated silicon, warmed water, contested labour markets and 30 tonnes of gold a year in e-waste.
